q: The platoon conducted a reconnaissance mission near the border. “Reconnaissance” means:
e: Reconnaissance = observing an area to collect intelligence (recon).

q: The two sides finally agreed to a ceasefire. A “ceasefire” is:
o: a temporary stop in the fighting
e: Ceasefire = suspension of hostilities.

q: Additional troops were deployed to the region. “Deployed” means:
e: To deploy = to move forces into position.

q: The enemy suffered heavy casualties. “Casualties” are:
e: Casualties = personnel killed, wounded, or missing.

q: Morale among the sailors was very high. “Morale” means:
e: Morale = the mental and emotional condition of a group.

q: The soldiers returned to their barracks after the exercise. “Barracks” are:
e: Barracks = military housing for personnel.

q: He was promoted to a higher rank. A “rank” is:
o: a position in the military hierarchy
e: Rank = official grade (petty officer, commander, major...).

q: The unit will withdraw at dawn. “Withdraw” means:
e: To withdraw = to retreat / move back.

q: Logistics is critical to any campaign. “Logistics” refers to:
o: the supply and movement of troops and equipment
e: Logistics = planning and moving personnel, supplies, and equipment.

q: The patrol was caught in an ambush. An “ambush” is:
o: a surprise attack from a hidden position
e: Ambush = a surprise attack by concealed forces.

q: The colonel issued new orders this morning. “Issued” means:
e: To issue orders = to give them officially.

q: The area is under constant surveillance. “Surveillance” means:
e: Surveillance = continuous watching of a person, place, or activity.

q: He is on leave this week. “Leave” means:
e: Leave = official permission to be absent (vacation).

q: The fleet set sail at dawn. A “fleet” is:
e: Fleet = a large group of ships under one command.

q: The recruits completed basic training. “Recruits” are:
e: Recruit = a person who has recently joined the armed forces.

q: Hostilities ceased at midnight. “Ceased” means:
e: To cease = to stop.

q: They reinforced the position overnight. “Reinforced” means:
o: strengthened with additional troops or material
e: To reinforce = to make stronger with extra forces or support.

q: An NCO briefed the squad. An “NCO” is:
o: a non-commissioned officer, such as a petty officer
e: NCO = Non-Commissioned Officer (corporal, petty officer...).

q: The mission was aborted due to bad weather. “Aborted” means:
e: To abort = to stop an operation before it is finished.

q: The frigate is on patrol in the strait. “Patrol” means:
o: moving through an area to watch and protect it
e: To patrol = to move around an area to monitor or secure it.

q: The convoy reached the port safely. A “convoy” is:
o: a group of vehicles or ships traveling together
e: Convoy = vehicles/ships moving together, often under escort.

q: The officer was court-martialed. “Court-martialed” means:
e: Court-martial = a military trial for offenses against military law.

q: The army mobilized within 48 hours. “Mobilized” means:
o: assembled and prepared forces for action
e: To mobilize = to prepare and organize troops for active service.

q: The crew practiced the fire drill again. A “drill” is:
e: Drill = practice through repetition.

q: The squad took cover behind the wall. “Took cover” means:
e: To take cover = to shelter from enemy fire.

q: They underestimated their adversary. An “adversary” is:
e: Adversary = opponent, enemy.

q: Follow the chain of command. The “chain of command” is:
e: Chain of command = hierarchy through which orders pass.

q: I need to stop for gas before we hit the highway. In American English, “gas” means:
e: Gas = gasoline (petrol in British English).

q: Take the elevator to the fifth floor. An “elevator” is:
o: a machine that carries people between floors
e: Elevator (*US*) = lift (UK).

q: We rented an apartment downtown. “Downtown” means:
e: Downtown = the central business district of a city.

q: He is on vacation until Monday. “Vacation” means:
e: Vacation (*US*) = holiday (UK).

q: Please email me your résumé. A “résumé” is:
o: a summary of your education and work experience
e: Résumé (US) = CV (UK): a summary of your education and work experience.

q: Walk on the sidewalk, not in the street. A “sidewalk” is:
e: Sidewalk (*US*) = pavement (UK).

q: The faucet in the kitchen is leaking. A “faucet” is:
o: a tap that controls water flow
e: Faucet (*US*) = tap (UK).

q: Classes start in the fall. “Fall” means:
e: Fall (*US*) = autumn.

q: My schedule is completely full this week. A “schedule” is:
o: a plan of times for activities
e: Schedule = timetable, planned program.

q: She was really mad at her brother. Here, “mad” means:
e: In American English, mad = angry.

q: I finally figured out the problem with the radio. “Figured out” means:
e: To figure out = to understand or find the solution.

q: Can you give me a ride to the base? A “ride” is:
o: a trip in a vehicle, as a passenger
e: Give someone a ride (*US*) = give someone a lift (UK).

q: The store is two blocks away. A “block” is:
o: a section of street between two intersections
e: Block = the distance between two street corners.

q: He bought candy for the kids. “Candy” means:
e: Candy (*US*) = sweets (UK).

q: The movie starts at eight. A “movie” is:
e: Movie (*US*) = film.

q: Toss it in the trash. “Trash” means:
e: Trash (*US*) = rubbish (UK).

q: I'll call you on my cell. A “cell” here is:
e: Cell (cell phone) = mobile phone.

q: He ordered a burger with french fries. “French fries” are:
e: French fries (*US*) = chips (UK).

q: Would you like a cookie with your coffee? A “cookie” is:
o: a small, flat, sweet baked treat
e: Cookie (US) = biscuit (UK). In American English, a *biscuit* is a small soft bread roll.

q: The restroom is down the hall on the left. A “restroom” is:
e: Restroom (*US*) = public toilet.

q: I bought a round-trip ticket to Washington. “Round-trip” means:
e: Round-trip (*US*) = return ticket (UK).

q: He works the graveyard shift at the harbor. The “graveyard shift” is:
e: Graveyard shift = work period during the night (e.g., midnight–8 a.m.).

q: That new destroyer is awesome! “Awesome” means:
e: Awesome (*US*, informal) = great, excellent.

q: I guess you're right about the schedule. “I guess” means:
e: I guess (*US*) = I suppose.

q: A “sortie” is:
o: a single operational flight by one aircraft
e: Sortie = one operational flight by a single aircraft.

q: “Attrition” refers to:
o: gradual reduction of strength through losses
e: Attrition = the gradual wearing down of forces.

q: A “beachhead” is:
o: a position secured on a hostile shore
e: Beachhead = a position secured on an enemy shore.

q: “Ordnance” means:
e: Ordnance = weapons and ammunition.

q: A “detachment” is:
o: a small unit sent on a separate duty
e: Detachment = a small unit sent away on a separate duty.

q: “Reconnaissance in force” means:
o: an attack made to obtain information
e: Reconnaissance in force = an attack made to find out the enemy's strength and positions.

q: A “contingency plan” is:
o: a plan for a possible future event
e: Contingency plan = a plan ready for a possible future event.

q: “Force projection” means:
o: deploying military power at a distance
e: Force projection = deploying military power far from home.

q: “Deterrence” is:
o: preventing action through fear of consequences
e: Deterrence = preventing action through fear of the consequences.

q: A “task force” is:
o: a temporary grouping for a specific mission
e: Task force = a temporary grouping of units for a specific mission.

q: A “no-fly zone” is:
e: No-fly zone = airspace where flights are prohibited.

q: “Collateral damage” means:
o: unintended harm to civilians or property
e: Collateral damage = unintended harm to civilians or property.

q: “Chain of custody” refers to:
e: Chain of custody: the documented handling of evidence.

q: “Standing orders” are:
e: Standing orders = permanent instructions.

q: A “quartermaster” is responsible for:
e: Quartermaster = the person responsible for supplies and provisions.

q: “Escalation” means:
e: Escalation = an increase in intensity.

q: “Situational awareness” means:
o: understanding what is happening around you
e: Situational awareness = understanding what is happening around you.

q: An “embargo” is:
e: Embargo.

q: “Rules of engagement” determine:
o: when and how force may be used
e: Rules of engagement = rules on when and how force may be used.

q: “Chokepoint” means:
o: a narrow passage that can be blocked
e: Chokepoint = a narrow passage (a strait, a pass, a bridge) that is easy to block.

q: A “briefing” given after an operation is a:
e: Debriefing.

q: “Sustainment” refers to:
o: keeping forces supplied and effective over time
e: Sustainment over time.

q: “To relieve” a unit means:
e: To relieve a unit = to replace it with another unit in its position, so that it can rest or move elsewhere.

q: “Hardware” in a defense context means:
e: Hardware (defense) = military equipment.

q: “Surge capacity” means:
o: the ability to increase output rapidly
e: Surge capacity = the ability to increase output quickly.

q: The briefing on the new leave policy is for *enlisted* personnel only; officers will get theirs at 1400.
o: serving in ranks below the officers
working on the base as civilian staff
e: Enlisted members are service members who are not officers: privates, corporals, sergeants and so on.

q: After four years at the academy, she was ______ as a second lieutenant in the Air Force.
e: Officers are commissioned: they receive their rank through an official commission. Enlisted members enlist; draftees are drafted.

q: A colonel ______ a major, so the major salutes first when they meet outdoors.
e: To outrank = to hold a higher rank than someone. A colonel is above both a lieutenant colonel and a major.

q: New recruits must learn to recognize the rank ______ worn on the collar, the sleeve or the chest of each uniform.
e: Insignia = badges or symbols that show a person's rank, unit or specialty.

q: The day after his promotion to sergeant, he sewed the new *chevrons* onto his dress uniform.
o: small metal badges awarded for good shooting
cloth tapes printed with his last name
e: Chevrons are the V-shaped stripes that mark the rank of corporals and sergeants.

q: After the drunk-driving arrest, the corporal was ______ to private first class and lost part of his pay.
e: To demote = to lower someone's rank (the opposite of promote). Deported = sent out of a country.

q: After four years in the Marines, he received an honorable ______ and used his GI Bill benefits to attend college.
e: A discharge is the official release from military service; 'honorable discharge' is the fixed expression.

q: As a *reservist*, Ms. Grant drills one weekend a month and trains for two weeks every summer.
o: a part-time member of the armed forces
a retired officer who advises commanders
a clerk who books training areas
a soldier waiting for a medical board
e: A reservist is a civilian most of the time who trains part-time and can be called to active duty.

q: When a Marine twisted his ankle on the hike, the *corpsman* wrapped it and checked the blood flow to his foot.
o: a Navy medic attached to the unit
the soldier who carries the platoon radio
the officer who planned and led the hike
a military police officer on patrol
e: U.S. Marines get medical care in the field from Navy hospital corpsmen (pronounced 'core-man'), who act as their medics.

q: As the ______ officer, Captain Dubois kept the French and American headquarters informed of each other's plans.
e: A liaison officer is the link between two units or organizations and keeps each one informed about the other.

q: General Morris came into the room, followed by his ______, who carried his briefcase and his schedule for the day.
e: An aide (with -e) is a person, often a junior officer, who assists a senior officer. 'Aid' means help or assistance.

q: All ______ must report to the gym at 1300 for the annual safety briefing.
e: Personnel (noun) = the people who work in an organization. Personal (adjective) = private, belonging to one person.

q: While Captain Wells is on leave, Lieutenant Ruiz will serve as the ______ company commander.
e: Acting = doing a job temporarily in place of the person who normally holds it.

q: Make sure the hangar is spotless; some of the *brass* from headquarters will visit on Friday.
e: Informal American usage: 'the brass' or 'the top brass' = high-ranking officers.

q: A ______ usually consists of three or four squads and is led by a lieutenant, assisted by an experienced sergeant.
e: U.S. Army units from small to large: squad, platoon (3-4 squads), company, battalion, brigade, division.

q: The *sentry* at the fuel point stopped the truck and asked the driver for the password.
e: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep watch and control who passes; a common synonym is 'guard'.

q: Fill your *canteen* before we step off; there is no water point until the halfway mark.
o: a small bottle for carrying water
the snack bar where soldiers buy drinks
a cooking pot used in the field
a side pocket on the pack
e: In American military English, a canteen is a soldier's water bottle. (It can also mean a cafeteria, but not here.)

q: Each soldier carried a 35-pound ______ on his back during the twelve-mile road march.
e: A rucksack (or 'ruck') is a large backpack. A holster holds a pistol; a helmet is worn on the head.

q: The recruits took off their dress uniforms and put on *fatigues* for the afternoon field training.
e: Fatigues (plural) are the uniform worn for daily work and field duty, not the feeling of fatigue.

q: The team used branches and netting to ______ the vehicles so they could not be seen from the air.
e: To camouflage = to hide something by making it look like its surroundings.

q: From the top of the hill, the lieutenant studied the valley through his *binoculars*.
o: a two-lens device for seeing far
a radio for talking over long distances
a case that keeps maps dry
a device that shows your exact position
e: Binoculars make distant objects look closer; you look through them with both eyes.

q: Before the parachute jump, the sergeant checked that every soldier was wearing his *dog tags*.
o: metal ID tags worn on a chain
small pets kept as unit mascots
e: Dog tags are the small metal identification tags, with a soldier's name and basic data, worn around the neck.

q: The medics placed the injured driver on a *litter* and carried him to the waiting helicopter.
o: a pile of trash by the road
a small cart pulled by hand
e: In military and medical use, a litter is a stretcher. In everyday English, litter also means trash left in public places.

q: When the power went out, the ______ started automatically and kept the command post running.
e: A generator is a machine that produces electricity, usually driven by a fuel engine.

q: The cooks in the ship's *galley* prepare more than a thousand meals a day.
e: A galley is the kitchen on a ship or an aircraft (not 'gallery', a place to show art).

q: In the field hospital tent, the patients slept on folding *cots* instead of real beds.
e: In American English, a cot is a narrow folding bed. (In British English it is a baby's bed, which Americans call a crib.)

q: If your GPS stops working, use your map and ______ to find north and stay on course.
e: A compass is an instrument with a needle that points to magnetic north.

q: Each soldier was issued three days of field ______ before the unit left for the exercise.
e: Rations = fixed amounts of food given to each soldier, such as packaged field meals.

q: The ship took on fresh *provisions* in Naples before sailing east for six weeks at sea.
e: Provisions (plural) = supplies of food and drink, especially for a journey. In a contract, a provision is a condition.

q: The damaged trucks were sent back to the *depot* to be repaired and repainted.
o: a parking area by the front gate
e: A depot is a place where supplies and equipment are stored and serviced. In American English it can also mean a bus or train station, but not here.

q: The supply sergeant submitted a ______ for twenty new radios and a box of spare batteries.
e: A requisition is an official written request for supplies or equipment.

q: The base keeps a ______ of bottled water, blankets and tents in case a hurricane hits.
e: A stockpile is a large supply stored for future use or for emergencies.

q: Batteries, paper and tape are *expendable* items, so the unit does not have to account for each one after use.
e: Expendable items are consumed when used, so they are not returned or tracked one by one like durable equipment.

q: The platoon sergeant is held ______ for every piece of equipment signed out to the platoon.
e: To be held accountable for something = to be responsible for it and have to explain any loss. An accountant is a person.

q: Check the passenger *manifest* again; the loadmaster says one soldier is missing.
o: the boarding area at the airfield
the ticket given to each traveler
e: A manifest is the official list of the passengers or cargo on a ship, plane or truck.

q: On hot days at high altitude, the helicopter's *payload* must be reduced for safety.
o: the fuel it burns per hour
e: Payload = the load (people or cargo) an aircraft or vehicle carries. Hot, thin air gives less lift, so less weight can be carried.

q: Headquarters will ______ the remaining fuel to the units with the longest drive back to base.
e: To allocate = to give out a share of something (money, fuel, time) for a particular purpose.

q: Report to the *motor pool* at 0600 to sign out your vehicle for the convoy.
o: where unit vehicles are parked and maintained
a list of drivers who are available for duty
the fuel station near the main gate
the office that issues driver's licenses
e: A motor pool is the area where a unit keeps, services and dispatches its vehicles.

q: The brake parts are on *backorder*, so the truck will stay in the shop for another two weeks.
o: ordered but not yet in stock
returned to the seller for a refund
e: On backorder = ordered, but the supplier does not have it in stock yet; it will be delivered later.

q: The convoy stopped at the halfway point to ______ before crossing the desert.
e: To refuel = to fill a vehicle or aircraft with fuel again.

q: With the roads flooded, helicopters were used to ______ food and water to the cut-off villages.
e: To airlift = to carry people or supplies by aircraft, especially in an emergency.

q: The fuel trucks are ______ route to the airfield and should arrive within the hour.
e: En route (from French) = on the way. 'On route' is a common mistake.

q: Sergeant Kim just received *orders* for Korea and will leave in June.
o: official notice of a new assignment
a list of items to buy before leaving
requests from his family to stay home
instructions on how to behave abroad
e: In the military, 'orders' (plural) is the official document that assigns a service member to a new place of duty.

q: The colonel ______ the captain's order to move the trucks, so they stayed where they were.
e: To countermand an order = to cancel it by giving a new order. To countersign = to add a second signature.

q: Only the company commander can ______ the use of government vehicles on weekends.
e: After the modal 'can' we need a verb: authorize = officially permit.

q: Inspectors checked the unit's ______ with the new fire safety regulations.
e: Compliance with a rule = obeying it. A compliment is praise; a complement completes something.

q: The new uniform policy is ______ immediately, so wear the new patches starting today.
e: Effective immediately = in force from now. Efficient means working well without waste.

q: Because of the water leak, the base pool is closed *until further notice*.
o: until a new announcement is made
until the end of the week
until someone sends a written request
e: Until further notice = until you are told otherwise; no end date is given.

q: He set up an *allotment* so that part of his monthly pay goes straight to his wife's bank account.
o: a part of pay sent automatically
a small garden rented from the town
a pay increase for married soldiers
a loan approved by the base bank
e: A pay allotment is a fixed amount of a service member's pay sent automatically to a person or account every month.

q: The rescue team is on ______ and can take off within thirty minutes if the call comes.
e: On standby = ready to act at once if needed.

q: Please *acknowledge* this message as soon as you receive it.
o: pass it on to the other units
e: To acknowledge a message = to reply that you have received it.

q: When the platoon leader radioed, 'Move to Checkpoint 3 and wait,' the squad leader answered, '*Wilco*.'
o: I am unable to do that
e: Wilco is radio language for 'will comply': I received your message and I will do it.

q: After several fights, that bar downtown was declared *off-limits* to all service members.
o: a place they must not enter
a place used for official events
e: Off-limits = forbidden to enter; a commander can put a business or an area off-limits.

q: The company's *objective* was to reach the bridge by dawn and hold it until the engineers arrived.
o: the goal it had to achieve
the route it was told to follow
e: As a noun, objective = the aim or target of an operation. As an adjective it means unbiased, which does not fit here.

q: The engineers traveled with the *vanguard* so they could clear any obstacles from the road ahead.
o: the front part of a column
the last vehicles of a convoy
e: The vanguard is the part of a force that moves at the front (the opposite of the rear guard).

q: The two patrols left by different routes and will *rendezvous* at the old bridge at 2200.
e: To rendezvous (RON-day-voo) = to meet at a time and place agreed in advance.

q: The instructor told us to walk on a *bearing* of 090 degrees until we reached the stream.
o: the load carried by each soldier
e: A bearing is a direction given as an angle from north; 090 degrees is due east.

q: Soldiers in *airborne* units get extra pay because their training is more dangerous.
o: in charge of air traffic control
e: Airborne units are trained to be delivered into an area by parachute; jumping earns extra hazardous-duty pay.

q: The company completed a twenty-mile *forced march* in less than eight hours.
o: a fast march with few rests
a march ordered as a punishment
e: A forced march is a march at a faster pace or over a longer distance than normal, with few rest stops.

q: Make sure your gear is *squared away* before the colonel walks through the barracks.
e: Squared away (American military slang) = neat, organized and ready; said of a person, it means competent and well prepared.

q: He was charged with *insubordination* and lost half a month's pay.
e: Insubordination = refusing to obey a lawful order, or showing disrespect to a superior.

q: The *citation* read at the ceremony described how the sergeant pulled two drivers from a burning truck.
o: the official text of an award
a ticket for a traffic violation
a quotation from a famous book
e: An award citation is the official text describing what the person did to earn a decoration. Elsewhere it can mean a traffic ticket or a quotation.

q: Recruits on cleanup duty had to scrub the *latrines* every morning before breakfast.
o: the sleeping areas in the barracks
e: A latrine is a toilet, or a toilet area, in a military camp or barracks.

q: Private Brown was assigned to a cleanup *detail* for arriving late at morning PT.
o: a list of rules to follow
e: In the military, a detail is a small group (or one person) assigned to a particular task, such as a cleanup detail.

q: The entire crew was ordered to *muster* on the flight deck at 0800 for the captain's announcement.
o: clean the deck from end to end
line up to receive their pay
e: To muster = to gather (troops or a crew), usually to be counted, inspected or briefed.

q: The camp went quiet after *taps*, and nobody was allowed to leave the barracks.
o: the bugle call for lights out
the evening meal in the mess hall
the closing of the main gate
e: Taps is the bugle call played at the end of the day for lights out (and at military funerals).

q: Vehicles waited in the *staging area* until it was their turn to load onto the ship.
o: a gathering point before a move
e: A staging area is where troops and equipment assemble and get organized before the next stage of a movement.

q: If you feel ill tomorrow, go to *sick call* at 0630 instead of reporting for PT.
o: the daily time to see a medic
a phone call to your family
an official list of soldiers on leave
e: Sick call is the set time, usually early morning, when soldiers who are ill or injured can be seen at the clinic.

q: *Chow* will be served in the field at 1800, so bring your mess kit.
e: Chow is informal American (especially military) English for food or a meal; the dining facility is often called the chow hall.

q: We buy our groceries at the *commissary* because the prices are lower than in town.
e: The commissary is the supermarket on a U.S. military installation; the exchange (PX or BX) sells other goods.

q: The hospital and the gym are the two busiest buildings on the *installation*.
o: the new equipment being put in
e: In U.S. military English, an installation is a base or post. In everyday English it also means the act of installing something.

q: Captain Lee's first *tour of duty* was two years in Germany with an aviation brigade.
o: a period of service in one post
e: A tour of duty is a period of time spent serving in a particular place or job.

q: Two guards were *posted* at the entrance to the fuel storage area.
e: To post a guard = to station him at a particular place to keep watch.

q: After the morning announcements, the first sergeant shouted, '*Dismissed!*'
e: 'Dismissed' as a command ends the formation: soldiers may go. It does not mean they are fired.

q: Turn in your leave form at the *orderly room* before noon on Thursday.
o: a very clean and tidy room
e: In the U.S. Army, the orderly room is the company's administrative office, where the first sergeant and the clerks work.

q: Because of his knee injury, he is on a *profile* and cannot run for six weeks.
o: a page on a social media site
a side view of a person's face
a short description of a person
e: In the U.S. Army, a (medical) profile is a written order from a doctor that limits the physical activities a soldier may do.

q: A bridge was closed for repairs, so the convoy had to make a forty-mile *detour*.
e: A detour is a different, usually longer, route taken because the normal road is blocked.

q: Guards walked the ______ of the camp all night, checking the fence for gaps.
e: Perimeter = the outer edge or boundary of an area. A parameter is a limit or factor; a diameter is a line across a circle.

q: Instead of returning to camp, the company set up a ______ under the trees and slept in the open.
e: A bivouac is a temporary camp in the field, often with little or no shelter.

q: The engineers cannot start repairing the bridge until the infantry has ______ the area around it.
e: To secure an area = to make it safe and under control. Ensure = make certain; insure = protect with insurance; assure = tell confidently.

q: Send the exact ______ of the landing zone so the pilot can find it on his map.
e: Coordinates = the numbers that give a precise position on a map or grid.

q: During the ______ exercise, Marines came ashore from the ships in landing craft.
e: Amphibious operations move forces from the sea onto land.

q: The full-dress ______ of the change-of-command ceremony will be held on Thursday afternoon.
e: A rehearsal is a practice of a ceremony or performance before the real event; full-dress = in the uniforms of the real event.

q: A military police vehicle will ______ the fuel trucks from the depot to the airfield.
e: To escort = to go with someone or something to protect or guide them.

q: Morning PT began with fifteen minutes of ______: push-ups, sit-ups and jumping jacks.
e: Calisthenics = exercises that use your own body weight, without equipment.

q: The barracks must be spotless by Friday, when the sergeant major comes for his monthly ______.
e: An inspection is an official check that rooms, equipment or uniforms meet the standard.

q: The commander was ______ with the young driver and gave him only a verbal warning for the minor accident.
e: Lenient = not strict; giving a light punishment or none at all.

q: Sleeping while on guard duty is considered ______ of duty and can lead to a court-martial.
e: Dereliction of duty = failing to perform one's duties, through neglect or on purpose.

q: Colonel Hayes is a highly ______ officer who has received the Silver Star and two Bronze Stars.
e: A decorated officer has received medals (decorations). Decorative = used to make something look attractive.

q: At the scene of the bus crash, the medics carried out ______ to decide who needed treatment first.
e: Triage = sorting injured people according to how urgently they need care.

q: Do not drink from that tank; it is not ______ water and is used only for washing vehicles.
e: Potable water is safe to drink. Portable means easy to carry.

q: Check the duty ______ on the bulletin board to see which weekend you have guard duty.
e: A duty roster is a list showing who does which duty and when. A rooster is a male chicken.

q: The bugle call known as ______ wakes the soldiers at 0530 and starts the duty day.
e: Reveille (REV-uh-lee in American English) is the morning bugle call that signals the start of the day.

q: Sailors were granted ______ while the ship was in port, but they had to be back aboard by midnight.
e: In the U.S. Navy, liberty is authorized time off ashore for a short period, shorter than leave.

q: The platoon stood in ______ for twenty minutes while the inspector checked every uniform.
e: In formation = arranged in ranks and lines, as soldiers stand for inspection or announcements.

q: Report to battalion ______ at 0900 tomorrow to receive your new assignment.
e: Headquarters (HQ) = the main office from which a unit is commanded.

q: Because of the thick fog, ______ was less than fifty yards and all flights were canceled.
e: Visibility = how far you can see, depending on the weather and the light.

q: During the exercise, a 2300 ______ was in force, and anyone found outside after that time was reported.
e: A curfew is a time after which people must stay indoors or on post.

q: My grandfather is a Korean War ______; he served as a radio operator in 1952.
e: A veteran is a person who has served in the armed forces, especially in a war.

q: She received a medal for ______ after pulling three soldiers out of the flooded river.
e: Valor (American spelling; British 'valour') = great courage, especially in danger.

q: Hang your dress uniform in the hall *closet* so it doesn't get wrinkled in your duffel bag.
o: a built-in cupboard for storing things
a narrow corridor between two rooms
a covered porch at the front door
a heated room for drying laundry
e: Closet (US) = a built-in cupboard or small storage room for clothes and other things (UK: wardrobe / cupboard).

q: The movers carried the ______ upstairs, but two of its drawers slid out and fell down the steps.
e: A dresser (US) is a chest of drawers for clothes; a couch, a recliner or a bookcase has no drawers.

q: Please don't park in our *driveway*; my wife has to get her car out of the garage at six.
o: the short private road up to a house
the lane reserved for buses on a street
the parking area behind an office
the narrow path between two houses
e: A driveway is the private road between the street and a house or its garage.

q: Our dog dug three holes in the back ______ while we were at work, and now the lawn looks terrible.
e: Yard (US) = the grassy area around a house (UK: garden); you cannot dig holes in a porch, a hallway or a driveway.

q: The streetlight shines into the bedroom all night, so we bought heavy *drapes* for the window.
e: Drapes (US) = long, heavy curtains that you open and close.

q: It gets cold in the dorm at night, so she brought a thick *comforter* from home.
e: Comforter (US) = a thick padded quilt for a bed (UK: duvet). 'Thick' and 'brought from home' rule out a person.

q: Instead of renting, the sergeant bought a two-bedroom ______ near the base and now pays a monthly fee to the homeowners' association.
e: A condo (condominium) is an apartment you own in a building whose shared areas are run by an association.

q: The rent is $1,200 a month, but *utilities* are extra, so budget another $200 for them.
o: repairs and maintenance done by the owner
e: Utilities = basic services for a home, such as electricity, water, gas and sometimes internet.

q: We pay our rent on the first of every month, yet our ______ still hasn't sent anyone to fix the broken heater.
e: The landlord owns the property, collects the rent and is responsible for repairs; the tenant is the one who pays rent.

q: When you move out, you'll get your *security deposit* back unless you've damaged the apartment.
o: money held to cover possible damage
a monthly fee for the building's guards
the cost of changing the door locks
e: A security deposit is money a tenant pays at the start of a lease; the landlord keeps it only to pay for damage or unpaid rent.

q: It's freezing in the office; could you turn up the ______ a couple of degrees?
e: A thermostat controls the heating or cooling; a thermometer only measures the temperature.

q: My phone is dead; is there an *outlet* near your desk where I can plug in my charger?
o: a store that sells goods cheaply
e: Outlet (US) = an electrical socket in the wall. It can also mean a discount store, but 'plug in' shows the meaning here.

q: The power went out during the storm, so we found our way down the dark stairs with a ______.
e: Flashlight (US) = a small battery-powered light you carry (UK: torch).

q: Could you change the baby's *diaper* while I warm up her bottle?
e: Diaper (US) = nappy (UK), the absorbent underwear a baby wears and that must be changed often.

q: She pushed the twins around the park in a double ______ while she went jogging.
e: A stroller (US) is a small seat on wheels for a baby (UK: pushchair / buggy); a cradle, a playpen and a high chair stay in one place.

q: *Broil* the salmon for about six minutes, until the top is nicely browned.
o: cook it under strong direct heat
boil it slowly in salted water
cut it into very thin slices
soak it in a spicy sauce
e: Broil (US) = cook under the top heating element of the oven (UK: grill).

q: Fry the onions in a large ______ over medium heat until they turn golden brown.
e: A skillet is a frying pan; a kettle boils water, a colander drains food and a ladle serves soup.

q: She keeps the *pantry* stocked with canned goods in case a winter storm cuts off the roads.
o: a small room or cupboard for food
a large cooler for frozen meat
a vegetable garden behind the house
e: A pantry is a small room or cupboard, usually next to the kitchen, where food is stored.

q: Don't pour bacon grease down the kitchen sink, or the drain will get ______.
e: Clogged = blocked, so water cannot pass through; cold grease hardens inside pipes.

q: Our apartment is on the *first floor*, so we never need to wait for the elevator.
o: the floor just above street level
e: In the US the first floor is at street level (UK: ground floor); the British 'first floor' is the American second floor.

q: The carpet is covered with dog hair, so please ______ it before our guests arrive.
e: Vacuum (US verb) = clean with a vacuum cleaner (UK also 'hoover'); you mop hard floors, not carpets.

q: Our washer broke, so I'm taking a load of uniforms to the *laundromat*.
o: a dry cleaner's that presses clothes
e: A laundromat (US) is a place with coin-operated washers and dryers that anyone can use (UK: launderette).

q: We asked a *realtor* to help us find a three-bedroom house near the base.
e: Realtor (US) = a real estate agent (UK: estate agent), who helps people buy, sell or rent homes.

q: The unit's holiday party will be a *potluck* this year.
o: a meal where each guest brings a dish
a party with a prize drawing
a formal sit-down dinner with assigned seats
a buffet paid for by the commander
e: A potluck is a shared meal to which every guest brings some food; it has nothing to do with luck or prizes.

q: We sold the kids' old toys and a bike at our *garage sale* last Saturday.
o: a sale of used items at a home
a sale of cars at a dealership
a store that sells tools and parts
e: A garage sale (also yard sale) is a sale of used household things held at someone's home.

q: If you clip this ______ from the Sunday paper, you'll get two dollars off a box of cereal.
e: A coupon is a printed ticket that gives you a discount on a product.

q: The tag said $20, but with *sales tax* I paid $21.40 at the register.
o: a charge added by the state
a tip left for the cashier
a fee for paying by card
e: In the US, sales tax is usually added at the register, so you pay more than the price on the tag.

q: The furniture store offers *layaway* on any item over $300.
o: holding an item while you pay in parts
free home delivery and assembly by staff
a discount for buying several items
a guarantee that covers future repairs
e: Layaway: the store keeps the item for you while you pay for it little by little; you take it home when it is fully paid.

q: Everything on the ______ rack is 70 percent off because the store needs space for next season's clothes.
e: A clearance sale sells old stock very cheaply to make room for new goods.

q: At forty dollars, that leather jacket is a *steal*.
o: a fake copy of a designer brand
e: Informal: a steal = something sold at a surprisingly low price, a great bargain.

q: Don't open the back of the TV yourself, or you'll void the *warranty*.
o: the maker's promise to repair it
the right to return it for any reason
the manual that came in the box
the insurance against theft at home
e: A warranty is the manufacturer's written promise to repair or replace a faulty product for a certain time; to void it = to make it invalid.

q: You can't run the PT test in combat boots; go change into your ______.
e: Sneakers (US) = sports shoes for running and training (UK: trainers).

q: These *pants* are too long in the leg, so I'll have them hemmed before the ceremony.
e: Pants (US) = trousers. In British English, 'pants' means underwear.

q: He wore a gray suit with a matching *vest* and a red tie to the wedding.
o: a sleeveless jacket worn over a shirt
a cotton undershirt worn under a shirt
a scarf tied loosely around the neck
a wide belt worn around the waist
e: Vest (US) = a sleeveless garment worn over a shirt, often part of a suit (UK: waistcoat). A British 'vest' is an undershirt.

q: The ______ on my parka is stuck halfway, so I can't get it open or closed.
e: Zipper (US) = zip (UK), the fastener with two rows of teeth that opens and closes a jacket.

q: She slung her *purse* over her shoulder and headed for the door.
e: Purse (US) = handbag. In British English a purse is a small wallet for coins.

q: Put the drinks on my ______; I'll pay for everything when we leave.
e: A tab is a running bill at a bar or restaurant that you pay at the end: 'Put it on my tab.'

q: I'll have a large iced coffee *to go*, please.
o: to take out and drink elsewhere
served in a ceramic mug at my table
in the smallest size you have
e: To go (US) = to take away (UK): you take the food or drink out of the shop.

q: I need to pick up some cough syrup and toothpaste at the ______ on the way home.
e: A drugstore (US) sells medicine, toiletries and small household items (UK: chemist's).

q: We grilled some *zucchini* with olive oil and garlic as a side dish.
o: a short, thick type of Italian pasta
e: Zucchini (US) = courgette (UK), a long green vegetable of the squash family.

q: Parking costs a dollar an hour, and the meter takes only one kind of coin: I need exactly four ______ for one hour.
e: A quarter is a 25-cent coin, so four make a dollar (a dime = 10 cents, a nickel = 5 cents, a penny = 1 cent).

q: Grab a bag of *chips* and some salsa for the game tonight.
o: plastic tokens used to play poker
e: Chips (US) = crisps (UK), thin crunchy snacks sold in bags; British 'chips' are French fries.

q: We're paying for the new refrigerator in twelve monthly ______ of $80.
e: Installments are equal payments made regularly until the full price is paid.

q: Can you *break* a fifty? The cab driver doesn't have any change.
o: lend it to me until next payday
pay the driver with it for me
put it into your bank account
e: Break a bill (US, informal) = give smaller bills or coins of the same total value for it.

q: Neither of us felt like cooking, so we ordered Chinese ______ and ate it in front of the TV.
e: Takeout (US) = takeaway (UK): food bought at a restaurant to eat somewhere else.

q: I'll move some money from savings into my *checking account* so the rent check doesn't bounce.
o: an account that checks your credit
a long-term account that earns interest
a retirement plan from your employer
e: Checking account (US) = current account (UK), used for everyday payments, checks and a debit card.

q: She buys most of her kids' clothes at a *thrift store*.
o: a shop selling cheap used goods
a store selling only famous brands
a store that stays open all night
a large warehouse for bulk buying
e: A thrift store sells secondhand clothes and goods, often for charity (UK: charity shop).

q: The salary isn't great, but the ______ are excellent: health insurance, a pension plan and three weeks of paid leave.
e: Benefits are what a job gives you in addition to pay, such as health insurance and paid leave.

q: Anyone who works more than forty hours a week gets paid ______ at one and a half times the normal rate.
e: Overtime = hours worked beyond the normal week, usually paid at a higher rate ('time and a half').

q: Talk to ______ if your direct deposit didn't arrive on the first of the month.
e: Payroll is the office that calculates and pays employees' salaries.

q: Throw the suitcases in the ______ and let's get on the road before the traffic gets bad.
e: Trunk (US) = boot (UK), the storage space at the back of a car.

q: He changed lanes without using his *blinker*, and the car behind him almost hit him.
o: the light that shows you are turning
the horn in the middle of the wheel
the small mirror on the driver's side door
the switch for the windshield wipers
e: Blinker (US, informal) = turn signal (UK: indicator), the flashing light that shows which way a car will turn.

q: A rock hit the ______ on the highway and left a long crack right in front of the driver's eyes.
e: Windshield (US) = windscreen (UK), the large front window of a vehicle.

q: We drove on the *interstate* all the way from Texas to Georgia without seeing a single traffic light.
o: a border post between two states
a toll bridge over a river
e: An interstate is a large US highway that connects states and has no traffic lights.

q: I left the car in the ______ behind the PX; it's the gray pickup in the third row.
e: Parking lot (US) = car park (UK), an open area where cars are parked in rows.

q: Our flight to Germany has a three-hour ______ in Atlanta, so we'll grab lunch at the airport.
e: A layover (US) is a stop between two connecting flights (UK: stopover).

q: You may bring one *carry-on* and one personal item, such as a backpack or a laptop bag.
o: a small bag taken into the cabin
a suitcase checked in at the counter
a ticket for an upgraded seat
e: A carry-on is hand luggage that you take with you into the plane's cabin.

q: After we land, meet me at ______ carousel 5; my duffel bag is always the last one out.
e: Baggage claim is the area of the airport where you collect your checked bags from a carousel.

q: Driving in Manhattan is a nightmare, so we took the ______ uptown; the station was right under our hotel.
e: Subway (US) = underground railway (UK: the Underground). A British 'subway' is a pedestrian underpass.

q: Always cross at the *crosswalk*, even when the street looks empty.
o: a marked place for walkers to cross
a bridge built above the road for cyclists
the strip in the middle of a road
e: Crosswalk (US) = pedestrian crossing / zebra crossing (UK).

q: There's been an accident at the ______ of Main Street and Fifth Avenue, so traffic is backed up.
e: An intersection is the place where two or more streets cross (UK: junction / crossroads).

q: The truck behind us was *tailgating* the whole way, so I moved over to let it pass.
e: Tailgate = drive too close behind another vehicle, which is dangerous and often illegal.

q: It was just a minor ______ in the commissary parking lot; nobody got hurt, but my bumper is dented.
e: A fender bender (US, informal) is a small car accident with little damage.

q: A witness wrote down the *license plate* of the car that hit the mailbox and drove off.
o: the dealer's name on the car
e: License plate (US) = number plate (UK), the metal plate that shows a vehicle's registration number.

q: We got a flat on the way to the base, so we pulled over and put on the ______.
e: The spare (tire) is the extra wheel carried in the car; a 'flat' is a tire that has lost its air.

q: The new bridge saves twenty minutes, but drivers have to pay a $5 ______ to cross it.
e: A toll is money paid to use a road or bridge; a fare is what a passenger pays on a bus, train or taxi.

q: He was fined $50 for *jaywalking* across Fifth Avenue in the middle of the block.
o: crossing a street illegally on foot
riding a bicycle on the sidewalk
parking in a lane reserved for buses
driving without wearing a seat belt
e: Jaywalking = crossing a street on foot where or when it is not allowed.

q: Four of us from the motor pool ______ to work to save on gas; we take turns driving.
e: Carpool = share a car to travel together, usually taking turns driving.

q: Pull over to the *curb* and I'll jump out here.
o: a sign showing the speed limit
e: Curb (US) = kerb (UK), the raised edge between the sidewalk and the street.

q: The sign outside the motel said 'No ______,' which meant every room was already taken.
e: A vacancy is an available room; 'No Vacancy' means the motel is full.

q: An accident on the beltway caused total *gridlock* during rush hour.
o: traffic so heavy that nothing moves
a failure of all the traffic lights
the closing of every highway exit
a police roadblock to check drivers
e: Gridlock = a traffic jam so complete that vehicles cannot move at all.

q: The old ______ crossing has no gates, so look both ways before you drive over the tracks.
e: Railroad (US) = railway (UK); a railroad crossing is where a road crosses train tracks.

q: I got a *ticket* for doing 70 in a 55 zone.
o: a notice to pay a fine
a reserved seat on the next bus
e: A (traffic) ticket is an official notice that you broke a traffic law and must pay a fine.

q: After flying from Kuwait to Texas, I had terrible ______ and kept waking up at 3 a.m. for a week.
e: Jet lag is tiredness and disturbed sleep after flying across several time zones.

q: Write the five-digit ______ at the end of the address, or the letter may be delayed.
e: A ZIP code (US) is the five-digit postal code (UK: postcode); an area code is part of a phone number.

q: He cut his hand badly on a broken bottle, so we rushed him to the *ER*.
e: ER (US) = emergency room (UK: A&E); the operating room, where surgery is done, is the OR.

q: This pharmacy won't sell you antibiotics without a ______ from your doctor.
e: A prescription is a doctor's written order for medicine; a recipe tells you how to cook something.

q: For a mild headache, an *over-the-counter* painkiller such as aspirin should be enough.
e: Over-the-counter (OTC) medicine can be bought without a prescription.

q: My blood pressure pills are almost gone; I need to call the pharmacy and order a ______.
e: A refill is a new supply of the same prescribed medicine.

q: She *sprained* her ankle when she jumped off the back of the truck, and now it's swollen.
o: hurt it by twisting it suddenly
broke one of the small bones in it
e: Sprain = injure a joint by twisting it, stretching the ligaments without breaking a bone.

q: The cut on his forehead was so deep that the doctor had to put in six ______.
e: Stitches are pieces of thread used to sew a deep cut closed; bandages are put on, not in.

q: His arm will be in a *cast* for six weeks while the bone heals.
o: a hard case that holds a bone still
a cloth sling that hangs from the neck
a group of actors in a play
e: A cast is a hard covering, of plaster or fiberglass, that keeps a broken bone in place.

q: This allergy medicine may make you ______, so don't drive or operate machinery after taking it.
e: Drowsy = sleepy; a medicine that causes drowsiness makes driving dangerous.

q: The smell of diesel fuel on the boat always makes me *nauseous*.
e: Nauseous (US) = feeling as if you are going to vomit.

q: After he touched poison ivy, an itchy red ______ spread up his arm.
e: A rash is an area of red, often itchy spots on the skin.

q: With my insurance, I only have a $20 *copay* each time I see the doctor.
o: the part of the cost the patient pays
a special discount given to military families
a fee for missing an appointment
the monthly cost of the insurance
e: A copay is the fixed amount the patient pays for each visit or prescription; the insurance pays the rest.

q: Stay home until your fever is gone; the flu is highly ______ in the first few days.
e: Contagious = easily passed from one person to another, which is why you should stay home.

q: Don't forget to get your flu *shot* before you deploy.
e: Shot (informal US) = an injection, as in a flu shot.

q: Our daughter has another ear infection, so I made an appointment with her ______.
e: A pediatrician (UK spelling: paediatrician) is a doctor for children; a dermatologist treats skin and an optometrist checks eyes.

q: All new hires must pass a *physical* before they start working at the warehouse.
e: A physical (US) is a medical examination that checks whether someone is fit for a job, a sport or service.

q: The knee surgery is done on an *outpatient* basis.
o: without staying overnight in a hospital
outside a hospital, in the patient's own home
by a surgeon from another hospital
for patients who have no insurance
e: Outpatient = treated at a hospital or clinic and allowed to go home the same day.

q: You'll need a tetanus *booster* every ten years.
o: an extra dose of a vaccine
a car seat for a small child
e: A booster is an additional dose of a vaccine that keeps the protection strong.

q: After her annual review, she got a *raise* of two dollars an hour.
o: a move to a higher rank
e: Raise (US) = pay rise (UK), an increase in salary or wages.

q: During the government shutdown, thousands of civilian employees were put on *furlough*.
e: Furlough = a period when employees are told not to work and are not paid, usually for a limited time.

q: Her *cubicle* is the third one on the left, next to the copier.
o: a small work space with low walls
a private office with a door
a metal locker for personal items
e: A cubicle is a small open work area separated from others by low partitions.

q: Keep all your receipts, and you'll be *reimbursed* for meals and lodging during the trip.
o: paid back for money you spent
charged a fee for the service
e: Reimburse = pay someone back for money they spent, for example on an official trip.

q: I took the afternoon off to run some ______: the bank, the post office and the dry cleaner's.
e: Run errands = make short trips to do small jobs such as banking, shopping or picking things up.

q: Most of the teenagers working at the burger place earn *minimum wage*.
o: the lowest hourly pay allowed by law
a salary paid once a month
the tips they get from customers
their pay before taxes are taken out
e: Minimum wage = the lowest pay per hour that an employer may legally pay.

q: Check your *pay stub* to see how much was withheld for federal taxes.
o: the statement that comes with your pay
the receipt you get for your rent
the form you fill out to request leave
the bank card for your account
e: A pay stub (US) shows your pay for the period and the amounts taken out (UK: payslip).

q: The trucking company plans to ______ fifty new drivers before the holiday season.
e: In American English you hire people but rent or lease cars and apartments.

q: The colonel rarely bends the rules, but he agreed to ______ an exception for the sergeant whose wife had just gone into labor.
e: make an exception = allow something that is not normally permitted.

q: Has anyone ______ arrangements for the visiting delegation's transportation from the airport?
e: make arrangements = plan and organize something in advance.

q: After a slow first week, the new recruits are finally ______ steady progress on the rifle range.
e: make progress = improve or move forward; 'do progress' is a common error.

q: Even a small monthly donation can ______ a real difference to the families at the shelter.
e: make a difference = have an important effect.

q: The totals in this spreadsheet don't ______ sense; they're higher than the sum of the individual items.
e: make sense = be logical or easy to understand.

q: Before he enlisted, my father ______ a living as a long-haul truck driver in Texas.
e: make a living = earn enough money to live on.

q: With no clear guidance from headquarters, the lieutenant had to ______ a judgment call about whether to continue the patrol.
e: make a judgment call = decide using your own judgment when no rule applies.

q: He tried to ______ amends for missing his daughter's recital by taking her out to dinner the next night.
e: make amends (for) = do something to correct a wrong you have done.

q: Our new battalion commander ______ a point of learning the name of every soldier under her command.
e: make a point of doing something = make a special effort to do it.

q: There's no need to ______ such a fuss; it's only a small scratch on the bumper.
e: make a fuss (about) = show too much worry or anger about something small.

q: We only have one free afternoon in San Antonio, so let's ______ the most of it and visit the River Walk.
e: make the most of = use an opportunity as fully as possible.

q: It took my son a few months to ______ friends after we moved to Fort Carson.
e: make friends = start friendships; 'do friends' is not English.

q: Before deploying, every soldier is encouraged to ______ a will and update the beneficiaries on their life insurance.
e: make a will = prepare the legal document that says who receives your property.

q: Stop making ______ and just tell me why the report wasn't on my desk this morning.
e: make excuses = give reasons, often false ones, to avoid blame.

q: When the supply truck didn't arrive, the platoon had to *make do with* cold rations for two days.
e: make do with = manage with something that is not ideal because nothing better is available.

q: Could you ______ me a favor and pick up my dress uniform from the cleaners on your way back?
e: do someone a favor = help someone with something they ask.

q: The hailstorm ______ serious damage to the hangar roof and two parked helicopters.
e: do damage (to) = cause harm; 'make damage' is a common error.

q: Before you buy a used car, ______ some research on its accident history and mileage.
e: do research (never 'make research').

q: I cooked dinner tonight, so it's your turn to ______ the dishes.
e: do the dishes = wash the plates, glasses, etc. after a meal.

q: The new mechanic ______ an excellent job on the transmission; the truck shifts like new.
e: do a good / an excellent job = do a piece of work well.

q: Photos simply don't ______ justice to the view from the top of Pikes Peak; you have to see it yourself.
e: do justice to = show the true quality of something.

q: As punishment for being late, the drill sergeant made the whole platoon ______ fifty push-ups.
e: do push-ups / sit-ups / exercises; 'made the platoon do' = forced them to do.

q: You look exhausted. A week away from the office would ______ you a world of good.
e: do someone (a world of) good = be very good for someone.

q: Before he turned his life around and became a youth counselor, Jake *did time* for car theft.
o: waited a long time to be tried
e: do time (informal) = spend time in prison.

q: If you ______ a mistake on the form, don't panic; just ______ your best to correct it neatly.
e: make a mistake, but do your best.

q: Every Sunday morning I ______ the laundry and then ______ the bed with clean sheets.
e: do the laundry (wash clothes); make the bed (arrange the sheets and blankets).

q: After a night shift at the gate, I usually ______ a short nap before picking up the kids from school.
e: take a nap = sleep for a short time during the day.

q: Service members should ______ advantage of the free tuition assistance program while they're still on active duty.
e: take advantage of = make good use of an opportunity.

q: On the overnight drive to Atlanta, my wife and I ______ turns behind the wheel every two hours.
e: take turns = do something one after the other.

q: As platoon leader, she ______ full responsibility for the communication error instead of blaming her radio operator.
e: take responsibility (for) = accept that something is your fault or your duty.

q: The installation is ______ steps to cut its electricity bill by twenty percent before next summer.
e: take steps = take action to deal with a problem.

q: The new leave policy ______ effect on January 1, so plan your vacation requests accordingly.
e: take effect = start to apply (a law, rule or medicine).

q: The planners failed to ______ the weather into account, and the airborne exercise had to be postponed.
e: take something into account = consider it when deciding.

q: When the company commander was injured, the first sergeant ______ charge until a replacement arrived.
e: take charge (of) = take control and responsibility.

q: Years of rotating night shifts have taken a heavy ______ on his health and his marriage.
e: take a (heavy) toll on = cause serious damage over time.

q: Remember to ______ your antibiotics with food, or they may upset your stomach.
e: take medicine / pills / antibiotics (not 'eat' or 'drink').

q: I kept glancing at my watch, but he didn't take the ______ and talked for another hour.
e: take the hint = understand what someone is suggesting indirectly.

q: The maintenance crew ______ great pride in keeping their aircraft spotless.
e: take pride in = feel satisfied with and care about something you do.

q: Our instructor ______ attendance at the start of every class, so don't be late.
e: take attendance (AmE) = check who is present.

q: Before requesting more supplies, the new supply sergeant *took stock of* what was already in the warehouse.
e: take stock of = carefully examine a situation or what you have.

q: Let's ______ a short break now, and while you rest, I'll ______ a few phone calls.
e: take a break; make a phone call (= call someone).

q: Sergeant, can I ______ a word with you after formation? It's about your leave request.
e: have a word with someone = speak to someone briefly, often in private.

q: I accepted the job in Anchorage, but now I'm having second ______ about moving so far north.
e: have second thoughts = start to doubt a decision you made.

q: Many new arrivals ______ trouble finding affordable housing near the base.
e: have trouble (doing something) = find it difficult.

q: I ______ a feeling we're going to hit traffic on the way to the airport.
e: have a feeling = think that something is likely.

q: You ______ a point; we should check the forecast before we drive up the mountain.
e: You have a point = what you say is reasonable.

q: Slow down! You'll ______ an accident if you drive that fast on this icy road.
e: have an accident ('make an accident' is a common error).

q: Could you ______ me a hand carrying these cases of MREs to the truck?
e: give someone a hand = help someone.

q: She ______ birth to twins at the base hospital last Tuesday.
e: give birth (to) = have a baby.

q: During a mass-casualty event, medics ______ priority to the most seriously wounded.
e: give priority to = deal with someone or something first.

q: She ______ her employer two weeks' notice before starting her new job in Seattle.
e: give (two weeks') notice = officially tell your employer that you are leaving.

q: Can you ______ me a ride to the PX after work? My car is in the shop.
e: give someone a ride (AmE; British English says 'a lift').

q: His excuse about the broken alarm clock sounded odd, but I decided to give him the benefit of the ______.
e: give someone the benefit of the doubt = believe someone although you are not sure.

q: The old wooden footbridge finally *gave way* under the weight of the equipment.
e: give way = break or collapse under pressure.

q: Rumors about the base closing have ______ rise to a lot of anxiety among local business owners.
e: give rise to = cause something to happen or exist.

q: My grandmother ______ us a surprise visit last weekend and brought a homemade apple pie.
e: pay someone a visit = visit someone.

q: At the end of the exercise, the colonel ______ her a compliment on the clarity of her briefing.
e: pay someone a compliment = praise them ('make a compliment' is a common error).

q: The city ______ tribute to the firefighters who lost their lives in the warehouse fire.
e: pay tribute to = publicly show respect and admiration for.

q: Hundreds of veterans lined the street to ______ their respects to the late general.
e: pay your respects = show respect, especially to someone who has died.

q: He had to ______ a $200 fine for parking in a fire lane.
e: pay a fine = pay money as a punishment.

q: The extra hours you spend on vocabulary now will *pay dividends* on test day.
e: pay dividends = produce advantages in the future.

q: If you ______ attention during the safety brief and ______ notes, you won't need to ask questions later.
e: pay attention; take notes.

q: My grandfather always ______ his promises, no matter how small they were.
e: keep a promise = do what you promised.

q: With so many last-minute schedule changes, it's hard to ______ track of who is on duty.
e: keep track of = stay informed about something that keeps changing.

q: Let's ______ in touch after you transfer to Germany; send me your new email address.
e: keep (or stay) in touch = continue to communicate.

q: Could you ______ an eye on my bag while I buy a ticket?
e: keep an eye on = watch something to make sure it is safe.

q: Two sailors ______ watch on the bridge throughout the night while the ship was at anchor.
e: keep watch = stay awake and look out for danger.

q: After the argument with his supervisor, Mark decided to *keep a low profile* for a few weeks.
e: keep a low profile = avoid attracting attention.

q: The armorer *keeps tabs on* every weapon that leaves the arms room.
e: keep tabs on (informal) = watch closely, monitor.

q: Even when the customer started yelling, the cashier ______ her cool and called the manager.
e: keep your cool (informal) = stay calm.

q: I must have ______ a cold on the flight home; I've been sneezing all morning.
e: catch a cold = become ill with a cold.

q: The engine ______ fire shortly after the truck left the motor pool.
e: catch fire = start burning; 'open fire' means start shooting.

q: From the ferry, we ______ a glimpse of the aircraft carrier as it left the harbor.
e: catch a glimpse of = see something for a very short time.

q: Stop for a minute and ______ your breath before the last part of the climb.
e: catch your breath = rest until you can breathe normally again.

q: We managed to ______ a few hours of sleep in the back of the truck before the night march.
e: catch some sleep (informal) = get some sleep when you have the chance.

q: Try to *catch the waiter's eye* so we can ask for the check.
e: catch someone's eye = attract someone's attention.

q: We sat in ______ traffic on I-95 for almost two hours this morning.
e: heavy traffic = a lot of vehicles on the road.

q: I need a cup of ______ coffee before the 0500 briefing.
e: strong coffee / tea = with a lot of flavor and caffeine.

q: Our daughter was running a ______ fever, so we took her to the emergency room.
e: a high fever (run a fever = have a fever).

q: We're on a ______ schedule, so there won't be any time for sightseeing in Washington.
e: a tight schedule = with very little free time.

q: Thank you for coming in on such ______ notice; I know it's your day off.
e: on short notice = with little warning.

q: That was a ______ call! The truck missed our car by just a few inches.
e: a close call = an accident or danger that was only just avoided.

q: Somebody stole a car in ______ daylight from the busy commissary parking lot.
e: in broad daylight = during the day, when people can easily see.

q: Can you give me a ______ estimate of how much the repairs will cost?
e: a rough estimate = an approximate calculation.

q: Poor sleep causes stress, and stress causes poor sleep; it's a ______ circle.
e: a vicious circle = a problem that causes another one, which makes the first worse.

q: The joint exercise is a ______ opportunity to practice working with allied forces.
e: a golden opportunity = an excellent chance that may not come again.

q: With a ______ heart, she said goodbye to the unit she had served in for twenty years.
e: with a heavy heart = feeling very sad.

q: There's a ______ learning curve with the new radio system, but most operators master it in a week.
e: a steep learning curve = a lot to learn in a short time.

q: Please bring a ______ copy of your orders to in-processing; a photo on your phone won't be accepted.
e: a hard copy = a printed paper version of a document.

q: I woke up with a ______ throat and a slight cough, so I went to sick call.
e: a sore throat = a painful throat.

q: We got a ______ tire on the way to the airport and nearly missed our flight.
e: a flat tire (AmE) = a tire with no air in it.

q: There is ______ competition for the few slots in the flight training program.
e: fierce (or stiff, intense) competition.

q: A ______ diet and regular exercise will help you pass the physical fitness test.
e: a balanced diet = the right amounts of different kinds of food.

q: The ______ question on everyone's mind was whether the deployment would be extended.
e: a burning question = a very important and urgent question.

q: The quiet mountain village stood in ______ contrast to the noisy city we had just left.
e: in stark contrast (to) = very clearly different.

q: Ever since high school, she has taken a ______ interest in military history.
e: take a keen interest in = be very interested in.

q: Everyone in the barracks room is expected to do their ______ share of the cleaning.
e: do your fair share = do the part that is reasonably yours.

q: The new commander made ______ changes to the training schedule during her first month.
e: sweeping changes = changes that affect many things.

q: When the wounded veteran finished his speech, the audience gave him a ______ ovation.
e: a standing ovation = applause from an audience that stands up.

q: Living right next to the airfield is a ______ blessing: a short commute, but constant noise.
e: a mixed blessing = something with both advantages and disadvantages.

q: Routine ______ of the vehicles takes place every Friday morning in the motor pool.
e: After the adjective 'routine' and before 'of', a noun is needed: maintenance (spelling: maintain → maintenance).

q: The commander was praised for her ______ action during the flood, which saved dozens of lives.
e: An adjective must describe the noun 'action': decisive (= quick and firm).

q: Field radios must work ______ in extreme cold, or units lose contact with headquarters.
e: An adverb describes how the radios work: reliably. Reliable is the adjective, reliability the noun, rely the verb.

q: Engineers worked through the night to ______ the old bridge before the tanks crossed it.
e: After 'to' we need a verb: strengthen (= make stronger). Strength is the noun.

q: Since the new fuel system was installed, the ______ of our trucks has improved by almost 20 percent.
e: 'the ___ of' needs a noun: efficiency. Efficient is the adjective, efficiently the adverb.

q: After an ______ 20-mile march, the recruits fell asleep the moment they reached camp.
e: An -ing adjective describes what causes the feeling (the march); -ed describes how people feel (the recruits were exhausted).

q: Young drivers who behave ______ on the road usually pay much less for car insurance.
e: An adverb modifies the verb 'behave': behave responsibly.

q: The new software will ______ clerks to process travel claims in half the time.
e: 'enable someone to do something' = make it possible. Able is an adjective (be able to).

q: Despite the bad weather, the rescue mission was a complete ______.
e: After 'a complete' we need a noun: success. Successful is the adjective, succeed the verb.

q: The new recruits looked ______ when the drill sergeant shouted two different commands at once.
e: After 'look' use an adjective; -ed adjectives describe how people feel: they looked confused.

q: Following ______ close to the vehicle in front is a common cause of accidents in a convoy.
e: An adverb (dangerously) is needed to modify the adjective 'close'.

q: The city plans to ______ the road to the main gate so that larger trucks can get through.
e: After 'to' we need a verb: widen (= make wider). Width is the noun.

q: When you plan a parachute jump, the ______ of the weather forecast can be a matter of life and death.
e: 'the ___ of' needs a noun: accuracy (= being exact and correct).

q: Under base regulations, it is ______ to park in spaces reserved for emergency vehicles, even for a few minutes.
e: After 'it is' we need an adjective: illegal (= against the law or rules). Illegally is the adverb.

q: The new instructor is ______ respected by both officers and enlisted personnel.
e: Highly (= very much) modifies the participle 'respected'. High is the adjective, height the noun.

q: Soldiers who fail to ______ on the rifle range this week will have to try again in March.
e: After 'fail to' we need the base form of the verb: qualify (= reach the required standard).

q: Soldiers' ______, such as spouses and children, may use the base clinic free of charge.
e: Dependents (plural noun) = family members supported by a service member; dependence means needing someone or something.

q: Admission to flight school is highly ______; only about one applicant in ten is accepted.
e: After 'is highly' we need an adjective: competitive (= hard to win or get).

q: Applicants should ______ have some experience with satellite communications.
e: Preferably (adverb) = if possible; it goes between 'should' and the main verb.

q: Could you ______ what you mean by 'as soon as possible'? Is that today or tomorrow?
e: After 'Could you' we need a base verb: clarify (= make clear). Clarity is the noun.

q: Nobody understood why the exercise had been canceled until the sergeant gave us a clear ______.
e: 'a clear ___' needs a noun: explanation. Note the spelling change: explain → explanation.

q: The training scenario was so ______ that some soldiers forgot it was only an exercise.
e: so + adjective + that: so realistic that ... (after 'was', an adjective is needed).

q: Before the vehicles tried to cross, divers checked the ______ of the river at three different points.
e: The noun of 'deep' is depth (like long → length, wide → width).

q: The captain had to ______ every expense in a written report to the finance office.
e: After 'had to' we need a verb: justify (= give good reasons for).

q: A ______ of spare parts has kept three of our helicopters on the ground this month.
e: 'A ___ of' needs a noun: shortage (= not enough of something). Shortly means soon.

q: When the order to jump came, the young paratrooper stepped out of the aircraft without a moment's ______.
e: 'a moment's ___' needs a noun: without a moment's hesitation = immediately.

q: Repairing the storm damage to the hangar roof will cost a ______ amount of money.
e: An adjective is needed before the noun 'amount': considerable (= large). Considerably is the adverb.

q: A longer report is not ______ a better report, so keep yours short and clear.
e: 'not necessarily' (adverb) = not always or not automatically.

q: The new online form should greatly ______ the process of requesting leave.
e: After 'should (greatly)' we need a base verb: simplify (= make simpler).

q: Much to his ______, the lieutenant's phone rang loudly in the middle of the change-of-command ceremony.
e: '(Much) to his + noun' expresses a reaction: much to his embarrassment. Note the double r and double s.

q: All vehicles in the convoy must be ______ with a first-aid kit and a fire extinguisher.
e: Passive 'be equipped with' = have the necessary items. Note the double p.

q: ______, the inspection has been moved to Thursday, but nobody has told the first sergeant yet.
e: A sentence adverb is needed at the start: apparently (= it seems, according to what people say).

q: During their first week, new arrivals should ______ themselves with the base evacuation routes.
e: 'familiarize yourself with' (verb) = learn about something. Familiar is the adjective.

q: In the commander's ______, the executive officer will be in charge of the battalion.
e: After a possessive (the commander's) we need a noun: absence. An absentee is a person who is absent.

q: Please keep me ______ of any changes to the flight schedule, even minor ones.
e: 'keep someone informed (of)' = give them the latest news. Informative means full of useful facts.

q: It ______ snows here in April, but the snow rarely lasts more than a day.
e: An adverb of frequency goes before the main verb: it occasionally snows (= sometimes).

q: With fuel running low, the logistics officer had to ______ the units that needed it most.
e: After 'had to' we need a verb: prioritize (= decide what is most important and deal with it first).

q: Corporal Ruiz takes great ______ in keeping her equipment spotless.
e: 'take pride in something' uses the noun pride; proud is the adjective (be proud of).

q: In summer, it is ______ to carry at least two extra quarts of water when hiking in the desert.
e: 'It is advisable to' = it is a good idea to. Advice is the noun, advise the verb.

q: The truck skidded off the icy road and into a ditch; ______, nobody was seriously hurt.
e: A sentence adverb is needed after the semicolon: fortunately (= luckily).

q: Investigators believe the fire ______ in the kitchen of the dining facility shortly after midnight.
e: The clause 'the fire ___' needs a past-tense verb: originated (= started).

q: The hurricane caused widespread ______ along the coast and closed two airfields for a week.
e: 'caused widespread ___' needs a noun object: destruction. Destructive is the adjective.

q: The constant beeping of the faulty alarm was extremely ______.
e: -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes the feeling: the noise was annoying (people are annoyed).

q: Families kept checking their phones ______ for news of the missing helicopter crew.
e: An adverb describes how they kept checking: anxiously (= in a worried way).

q: For this hike, each soldier's pack should ______ no more than 50 pounds.
e: After 'should' we need a base verb: weigh. Weight is the noun.

q: Months of careful ______ went into the joint exercise with our allies.
e: 'Months of careful ___' needs a noun: preparation.

q: The whole team was ______ with its result in the base volleyball tournament.
e: 'be disappointed with' describes how people feel; the result itself was disappointing.

q: The driver's ______ to wear a seat belt led to a formal warning from the military police.
e: After a possessive and before 'to + verb', a noun is needed: refusal. (The noun 'refuse' means garbage.)

q: Forecasters expect the storm to ______ overnight before it reaches the coast.
e: 'expect something to + verb': to intensify (= become stronger).

q: Every pilot completes a ______ course in case the aircraft goes down far from friendly forces.
e: A noun is used as a modifier here: a survival course. Survive is the verb.

q: Take a deep ______ and hold it while the technician takes the X-ray.
e: Breath is the noun (take a deep breath); breathe, with a final e, is the verb.

q: The inspector rated the condition of the barracks as ______, though far from excellent.
e: Satisfactory = good enough (describes things); satisfied describes how people feel.

q: The family readiness group is ______ looking for volunteers to help during the holidays.
e: An adverb modifies the verb 'looking': actively looking.

q: Wear a helmet and gloves at all times to ______ the risk of injury.
e: 'to + verb': minimize (= reduce to the lowest possible level). Minimum and minimal are not verbs.

q: The ______ of the only bridge would cut the main supply route in two.
e: 'The ___ of' needs a noun: loss. Lose is the verb, lost its past form.

q: The medic's ______ decision to run back into the burning vehicle earned her a medal.
e: An adjective is needed before the noun 'decision': courageous (= brave).

q: Because of the thick fog, the flight from Ramstein will ______ be delayed until noon.
e: An adverb goes between 'will' and the main verb: will probably be.

q: ______ the chin strap on your helmet before you climb into the vehicle.
e: An imperative sentence starts with a verb: tighten (= make tight).

q: At lunch, soldiers have a ______ between a hot meal and a boxed sandwich.
e: 'have a ___ between' needs a noun: choice. Choose / chose / chosen are verb forms.

q: This small car is very ______; it gets almost 50 miles per gallon on the highway.
e: After 'very' we need an adjective: economical (= saving money or fuel).

q: The patrol moved ______ through the forest, communicating only with hand signals.
e: An adverb describes how they moved: silently.

q: The long illness had ______ him so much that he could hardly climb the stairs.
e: Past perfect: had + past participle of the verb weaken (= make weak).

q: You will need ______ of residence to register your car on base.
e: '___ of residence' needs a noun: proof. Prove is the verb.

q: Tired workers are rarely ______, so the manager decided to cut the night shifts to eight hours.
e: After 'are (rarely)' we need an adjective: productive (= doing a lot of useful work).

q: Conditions on the ground changed so ______ that the intelligence briefing had to be updated twice.
e: 'so + adverb + that' modifies the verb 'changed': so rapidly that.

q: The children ______ very well during the long ceremony, so they got ice cream afterward.
e: The sentence needs a past-tense verb: behaved. Behavior is the noun.

q: Nobody may enter the ammunition storage area without written ______ from the range officer.
e: 'without written ___' needs an uncountable noun: permission. Permissible = allowed; permissive = too tolerant.

q: The weekend workshop is completely ______; nobody will be ordered to attend.
e: After 'is completely' we need an adjective: voluntary (= done by choice, not required).

q: Handle the night-vision goggles ______; each pair costs over three thousand dollars.
e: An adverb modifies the verb 'handle': handle carefully.

q: She was ______ to staff sergeant after only four years in the Army.
e: Passive: was + past participle: was promoted (= given a higher rank).

q: To avoid being tracked, the radio operator switched to a different ______ every few minutes.
